title: The watchers see the long back in the water
summary: Four men keeping the tower at Seann Skell watch a back long as three boats rise off the point in the failing light and go under without a sound. Their four tellings differ in every small particular but agree on the length and the silence.

title: Word of the sighting runs round the bay
summary: The tale of the tower's watch grows a head and a neck by the time it has gone twice round the bay of Seann Skell, though the old women of that coast say only that the sea shows itself when it chooses and take no boat off the water for the telling.

title: Stitched planks come ashore south of Seann Skell
summary: Through a season the wrack south of the tower gives up narrow stitched planks from more than one hull, shaped for open water and like nothing built on that coast, with not one scrap of cord, tool or bone to say what rode in them.

title: No household will claim the wreck
summary: Asked along the shore, no household admits to a boat of its own building broken among the planks, nor lacks a man, woman or child it cannot otherwise account for; the wreck stays a wreck with no name and no mourner.

title: Coinneach Beag lays the planks against his wall
summary: A fisherman of that coast, Coinneach Beag, gathers the stitched wood along one wall and pieces two curved lengths of hull back into shape, finding boats narrower and longer in the beam than any the coast builds for its own close fishing.

title: Anndra Breac comes to the wall of planks
summary: Anndra Breac, a teller who has walked the western shore twenty years and more without a household of his own, hears Coinneach Beag out and returns to look at the planking again by firelight more than once before the season turns.

title: Anndra shapes a fourth telling
summary: Turning the planks and the tower's tale over through the winter, Anndra comes to think a boat lost whole but for its wood argues not a wreck close to shore but a crossing once made, long before any telling now kept remembers the making of it.

title: The coast hears him out without agreeing
summary: Anndra tries the telling first on households that have fed him twenty years running; none of them denies it outright, and an old woman near Seann Skell tells him a tale a man cannot leave alone wants telling somewhere it will be properly heard.

title: Anndra Breac tells the crossing at the ford
summary: At the yearly gathering, by the largest fire he can get a footing at, Anndra Breac tells a telling in which the hill-folk crossed the sea in boats once and lost more of themselves to the crossing than any telling now remembers.

title: The crowd shouts him down
summary: An old man of a hill household calls out that no teller says the hill-folk came from anywhere, for they were always here, and others take up the shout until Anndra's own voice can no longer be heard over the fire.

title: Every hearth of Dia-thìr closes to him
summary: No household strikes him and none needs to; by the roads home from the ford it is already understood that Anndra Breac is not to be fed at a hill hearth again, and by the following spring not one has.

title: The king laughs once and falls quiet
summary: Standing near enough his own fire to hear the telling, the king laughs low at some point in it those nearest him cannot agree on afterward, does not join the shouting nor still it, and is seen quiet the rest of that evening in a way his own kin know to read.

title: The king will not choose between the tellings
summary: Asked afterward by a woman of his own kin whether the teller spoke true, the king answers only that he has heard many tellings of where his own people came from and has never troubled to choose one over another.

title: The saying is spoken at the opening of the gathering
summary: The gathering at the ford opens for the first time with the column's saying spoken aloud before any business begins, we did not come, we were here, a thing said together from that year rather than kept only in each hearth's own quiet belief.

title: Anndra Breac walks south along the western strand
summary: Seen once more below the tower at Seann Skell, walking the strand where the stitched planks still lie against Coinneach Beag's wall, Anndra Breac walks on and does not look back; no teller of that coast claims to have fed, spoken to or buried him after.
